book: 128 - Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood
essays: 1. The Wonderful Feeling of Being Alive
3. Wonder and Philosophy as a Way Home
4. The Gently Socratic Inquiry of Fred Rogers
13. Won’t You Be My Posthuman Neighbor
14. A Party to Celebrate the Personal
17. A Word from a Man Mister Rogers Ruined
19. If Everyone’s Special, … Is Anyone Special
samples: Editor Holly Mohr's introduction recounts receiving Plato's Republic and Apology for a summer program and realizing she had been philosophizing since childhood, and that Fred Rogers would not have been surprised: wonder is what children do best and what philosophy is. She argues Rogers takes children seriously as full persons, shows through his visits to workers, farmers, and children with disabilities that wonder is available in every life, and that meaning is made together in the Neighborhood, in community rather than solitude.

Jacob Graham reads the show's behind-the-scenes honesty (episode 1530's studio tour, Rogers showing the puppets dead in his bag) through Plato's Theaetetus claim that philosophy begins in the feeling of wonder and its call for the philosopher's leisurely slowness (skole), which Rogers built into television through silence and a low pace. Drawing also on Aristotle's Metaphysics, he argues wonder at the sheer being of ordinary things ends in reverent silence before each person's unrepeatable uniqueness, which Rogers treats as axiomatic: 'I like us just the way we are.'

Marlene Clark argues Fred Rogers was a mesmerist in the lineage of Franz Mesmer's animal magnetism, a hypnotic appeal that survived mesmerism's debunking by passing into Freud and Breuer's psychoanalytic transference and into the primitive, unconscious sex appeal of screen idols like Brad Pitt. She details episode 1588, where Rogers defuses bathtub-drain fears with 'You Can Never Go Down the Drain' and scuba-suited Neighbor Aber frightens Henrietta Pussycat, and the 1969 Senate hearing where reciting 'What Do You Do with the Mad That You Feel?' visibly entranced Senator Pastore into awarding PBS 20 million dollars.

Nathan and Leilani Mueller argue the theme song's 'neighborly day in this beautywood' makes beauty a transcendental leading to wisdom, as in Plato's Symposium ascent to loving the beautiful itself and Aquinas's convertibility of truth, goodness, and beauty. Reading Rogers's questioning of batteries and boxes (episode 1655) through the Meno's genuine curiosity and Pierre Hadot's account of philosophy as a way of life, they tour the show's three philosophical spaces: the domestic living room, the community visit (blind saxophonist Eric Kloss), and Make-Believe as thought experiment.

Ben Lukey and Steve Bein, veterans of p4c Hawai'i, argue Rogers ran a 'gently Socratic' community of inquiry on television: unlike Socrates the public gadfly who made asses of interlocutors, Rogers created intellectual safety, treating Daniel Striped Tiger's 'What does assassination mean?' (after MLK's murder) and the Officer Clemmons kiddie-pool scene as philosophy with children. Using Dr. Tom Jackson's Good Thinker's Toolkit to show children are philosophers, they defend 'little p philosophy' as activity over 'Big P Philosophy' as content, casting Rogers and Socrates as midwives rather than lecturers.

Sydney Ball and Eric Mohr interleave a college student's Tuesday with her six-year-old self watching the show: Plato's Republic (439c) on the rational part overruling the appetitive frames procrastination and lost youthful energy, Kant's autonomy frames doing what you should without being told, and Heidegger's 'They' frames her supermarket jealousy, dissolved by complimenting a stranger's shoes just as Henrietta Pussycat overcame jealousy of Grandpere's fancy granddaughter Collette (episodes 1176-1180). The lesson, learned from Mister Rogers's words about stopping, is authenticity: 'I like you just the way you are.'

book: 129 - RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought
essays: 4. Is It Immoral to Read Someone to Filth
7. The Sublime Sabotage of the Inner Saboteur
14. You Want Some Privacy You Better Work
samples: Kate Bornstein's foreword argues that Drag Race is the first pop phenomenon to present drag life and performance as a continuum rather than a one-night bar show, letting viewers watch queens learn their gender 'at the level of values' rather than rules. She frames drag as 'the proudly flamboyant performance of a broken binary' at the heart of postmodern gender theory, pointing to the casual pronoun shifts among contestants as theory in action. Quoting Season 11 winner Yvie Oddly on how different aesthetics show the possibilities of human experience, she casts both RuPaul and the show's contestants as gender royalty who embody values no one grew up with rules for.

The editors' introduction argues that Drag Race is an unexplored philosophical playground because it builds on marginalized black and Latinx queer herstory and because RuPaul, whose creed of love and self-improvement makes her a philosopher in her own right, has made the show her magnum opus. It invokes Plato's cave to explain why philosophers crave the 'untucked' version of everything RuPaul shows on stage. Its central move is a virtue-ethics reading of the show's judging: Ru's demand that a queen first be fierce, and through fierceness achieve charisma, uniqueness, nerve and talent, mirrors Aristotle's question of what makes a good person, with fierceness playing the role phronesis plays in securing the other virtues. Comparing queens like Silky Nutmeg Ganache, Jinkx Monsoon, Yara Sofia and Sharon Needles, it poses 'what makes a good drag queen?' as a live philosophical problem.

Volpert maps Baudrillard's four levels of simulacra onto Drag Race's 'realness': faithful copies (Trinity the Tuck's tucking tutorial, the Season 10 Cher challenge), distorted copies (Sasha Velour and Eureka's nerve, double wig reveals), simulations masking an absent reality (Vanjie's nonsense-word meme, Valentina replacing the judges' verdict with her own fantasy), and the pure hyperreal (Bob the Drag Queen as a queen made entirely by the show, BenDeLaCrème's self-elimination as uniqueness with no referent). She then argues RuPaul is a better Warhol because Warhol merely produced superstars like Candy Darling, Holly Woodlawn and Jackie Curtis, profiting while they died unmourned, whereas Ru could compete in her own challenges and returns love to her girls. Realness, she concludes with Ru's Billboard interview and the Season 3 'Pop Art Ball', is always a wink: the facade talking about facade.

McDonald takes Dorian Corey's Paris Is Burning definitions as the foundation for a speech-act analysis of reading versus shade in The Library challenge: reads require uptake from the target and state the insult as at-issue content (Jujubee's 'your grill is fucked up', Latrice's 'illiterate fuck'), while shade smuggles the insult in through implicature and presupposition without needing uptake (Bianca's 'What's your name again?', Aja's Valentina rant), with direct unplayful attacks like Shangela's sugar-daddy rant at Mimi Imfurst as a third category. She tests Plato's superiority theory, Kantian-style incongruity theory and relief theory to argue that a good read works as catharsis, letting queens laugh at the slurs and insecurities that wound them outside the werkroom. Comparing drag lingo to Polari, the secret language of 1950s British gay men, she shows language building solidarity and safety, and leaves the appreciation-versus-appropriation question for fans open.

Sznajder uses All Stars' winner-eliminates-you twist (Naomics Smalls cutting Manila, BenDeLaCrème quitting) to ask what a rational queen should do, grounding instrumental rationality in Hume's 'reason is the slave of the passions'. She runs the Ultimatum Game (Latrice rejecting a 99-to-1 split from Valentina), diminishing marginal utility (Trixie's twenty-dollar tip then and now), expected utility with the pink mystery box, and a Trixie–Shangela Prisoner's Dilemma in which rational utility-maximizers eliminate each other when cooperation would leave both better off. The clash between the normative theory and what queens and experimental subjects actually do leads her to the chapter's 'No Sure Thing Principle': Drag Race's plot twists always add an option game theory never modeled, as BenDeLaCrème saw.

Birnie stages Alexis Michelle's hurt at the Season 9 body-shaming reads against Bianca Del Rio's 'rolodex of hate' to ask whether reading is immoral. He surveys the philosophical ethics of humor — Plato's Philebus on laughter as malicious delight in others' self-ignorance, Hobbes's 'sudden glory', Schopenhauer on why ridicule hurts, the Stoics' ideal of never laughing, Aristotle's eutrapelia as the golden mean between vulgar buffoon and boor, the Spencer–Freud relief theory, and Bergson's laughter as society's corrective — before endorsing the play theory: reads are consensual mock-aggression, verbal sport honed by marginalized black and Latinx ball culture. From this he derives three guidelines (play signals and consent, timing and audience given the show's younger mainstream viewers, openness to challenge) and concludes Katya's bus-stop read of Roxxxy was acceptable while stereotype reads need care.

book: 130 - The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife
essays: 1. The Good, the Bad, and the Bureaucratic
2. How Can Torture Be This Funny
5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon
7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife
8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning
9. Send The Good Place to the Bad Place
10. A Love Story between Theory and Praxis
12. How the Fork Did I Get Here
13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts
14. Is Kant the Reason Everyone Hates Moral Philosophy Professors
17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place
19. Hinduism Gets More than Five Percent Right
samples: The editors' introduction recounts how Eleanor Shellstrop wakes in Michael's fake Good Place with the indecisive ethics professor Chidi as her reluctant guide, and argues the show is unique because philosophy is not a gag but the vocabulary the characters use to understand themselves and their predicaments. It frames the volume as extending Chidi's ethics lessons to the audience and sets out the book's terminological conventions for the show, the fake neighborhood, and the real Good Place.

Westfall uses Hannah Arendt's account of bureaucracy as 'rule by Nobody' to read the show's afterlife: the point system runs itself, and no one, not Michael, not Shawn, not even Judge Gen, has authority to alter the automatic calculation of a life's score. Because bureaucracies deprive everyone subject to them of the power to act and thereby invite violence, Chidi's 'Most Improved Player' plea for Eleanor and Michael's Season Two argument before Gen that the system is 'fundamentally flawed' amount to the only recourse Arendt leaves: resistance against the system itself.

Pavelich asks how a sitcom about torture can be funny, answering with incongruity theory and Bergson's view of comedy as social punishment, seen in Tahani paired with a silent monk and Michael failing 802 reboots. The centerpiece is 'The Trolley Problem': Michael drops Chidi into Foot's thought experiment so Chidi becomes the instrument of his own agony, and by Bernard Williams's principle the real wrongdoer is Michael, who set up the situation. Eternal torture works as comedy only because everyday crappiness is watched on a twenty-two-minute scale, and Eleanor's forgiveness of Michael after seeing the tortures in Janet's VR makes her the show's real moral hero.

Bromhall contends the Soul Squad's moral growth cannot earn them Good Place points, because the contextualist point system rewards only the happiness an action actually adds to the universe, as the two Dougs' rose gifts show. Using William James's conditions for morally valuable action, foreseeable consequences and no do-overs, he argues the afterlife is the wrong context for human action since Michael can rewrite reality and wipe memories at will. Ironically the humans' growth only makes Michael and the demons miserable, while Michael's own high-stakes, irreversible self-sacrifice meets all of James's conditions and so alone deserves The Good Place.

Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.

Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.

book: 131 - Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head
essays: A Seriously Mind-Blowing Book about Seriously Mind-Blowing Movies
1. Rights and Wrongs of Reversing the Snap
2. What Does Life Mean after the Snap
3. Confronting Grief in the Post-Snap World
4. Why Does Grief Hurt So Much
8. Time Travel and the Problem of Evil
9. With Infinite Power Comes No Responsibility
10. Natasha, Gamora, and the Soul Stone
15. Life Is a Laugh and Death Is a Joke
17. Life Unchecked Will Cease to Exist
samples: The introduction argues that all villains, real or fictional, share one trait: they treat people as mere objects to be used, which is why Thanos's Snap feels monstrous. It then springs the book's central provocation: since Thanos kills half of all life to save the rest of the universe from overpopulation, resource exhaustion, and destruction, he is 'actually a strictly moral being' from a utilitarian perspective. It frames the tension between using persons and respecting them (the grenade-jumping soldier who gives himself willingly versus those sacrificed without consent) and previews the volume's chapters on Thanos's morality and mind, time travel, and death.

Philip Mouch weighs consequences against rights to ask whether the Avengers were wrong to undo the Snap in Endgame. He imagines a survivor whose returned spouse finds her remarried, cataloguing displaced families, food shortages, and political turmoil, and argues these harms, however real, are outweighed by restoring the lives Thanos took. The deeper problem is Bruce Banner's wager with the Ancient One: removing the Time Stone dooms a branch reality on a 1-in-14,000,605 chance, gambling innocent lives without their consent, which resembles Thanos's non-consensual sacrifice of Gamora rather than the noble self-sacrifice of Hawkeye and Black Widow on Vormir. He concludes that two wrongs do not make a right: even for a noble end, risking countless lives tramples the rights of others.

This chapter reads four post-Snap Avengers as existentialist answers to how life keeps meaning after catastrophe. Tony Stark embodies Sartre's existence precedes essence, defining himself through free choice up to his final 'I am Iron Man' snap that erases Thanos and his army; the merged Professor Hulk lives Camus's Sisyphus, embracing the absurd and concluding 'all is well' after watching his own past rage; Captain America lives Levinas's ethics of the Other, from refusing to abandon brainwashed Bucky in Civil War to wielding Mjolnir to save Thor; and Ronin-era Hawkeye enacts Nietzschean nihilism until Black Widow's Vormir sacrifice, read through Zarathustra's burning in one's own flame, restores his meaning. The authors conclude Marvel's answer is affirmation: courage to affirm freedom, the Other, and life itself against Thanos as personification of genocide, climate change, and war.

Benjamin Carpenter applies Judith Butler's idea of grievability from Precarious Life and Frames of War to Endgame: lives matter insofar as they can be mourned, and Thanos renders his billions of victims ungrievable by scale, turning deaths into statistics beside white stone monuments Scott finds his own name on. Most Avengers turn away (Tony retreats, Thor kills Thanos and sinks into depression, Clint goes on a murderous rampage), but Natasha stays at her post, keeping agency and hope alive, which is what lets Scott find her and the team reassemble. Her willing self-sacrifice on Vormir makes her the moral opposite of Thanos, 'the ultimate egoist' who wraps genocide in the language of balance and kills only others, and the chapter asks why Tony's funeral gets a long communal mourning while Natasha is mostly forgotten.

J. Keeping argues grief hurts because the griever still inhabits the past world of meaning where the loved one lived, drawing on Heidegger's 'referential totality of significance' (the hammer's for-structure) and Ryle's knowing-how versus knowledge-that to show our emotional lives are skills learned by doing, not facts we can update at will. Thanos is the pathological case: emotionally stuck in Titan's collapse, he applies his genocidal 'solution' to every planet, even ones that are not overpopulated, while Tony models healthy grieving by trading the superhero life for a different one built around Pepper and Morgan and finding something to live for. Because our identities are constituted by our actions, meanings, and interconnections with others, losing loved ones is 'the affective equivalent of amputation,' which is why Cap's support group and Tony's funeral matter.

Duncan Gale asks whether Endgame 'gets time travel right,' using David Lewis's 'The Paradoxes of Time Travel' to explain personal time versus external time (Steve and Nebula meeting their past selves), causal loops (Tony quoting the saying about money and time back to Howard, who seemingly hears it first), and the grandfather paradox (Rhodey's baby-Thanos plan, which the existence of Nebula proves the Avengers would always fail to carry out). He traces Marvel's branching-timeline rule from Marvel Two-In-One #50 through the Ancient One's warning that removing a stone splits reality, and argues the film's moral is that the Avengers refuse quick resets and dutifully return the stones, while Thanos would shred the universe and rebuild a 'grateful' one. The chapter closes with Ivan Karamazov's challenge about building the edifice of human happiness on a tortured child's tears, which Thanos would accept and the Avengers refuse.

book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney
essays: Perry Mason and Philosophy The Case of the Awesome Attorney
1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy
4. The Case of the Other Renegade Refugee
5. The Case of the Witless Witnesses
6. The Facts Don’t Speak for Themselves
10. Trust and Temptation at the Office
11. When Is a Lawyer Not a Lawyer
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Mason is beloved because he personifies the ideal of objective, discoverable truth: in a legal system run by fallible, sometimes crooked lawyers and jurists (O.J. Simpson, Robert Blake, Casey Anthony), Mason cuts through false accusations and frame jobs to vindicate the innocent, just as the Innocence Project and the Brian Banks story do in real life. It frames the whole volume by casting philosophers and Mason as fellow truth-seekers who believe an objective truth is 'out there' and that the law is a transcendent, unchanging thing beyond the reach of the people who muck it up, and closes with a tribute to Barbara Hale, TV's Della Street.

Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.

Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.

Scalambrino compares Mason and Better Call Saul's Saul Goodman, who pull the same shady moves (Perry's evidence switching in 'The Case of the Crimson Kiss' and 'The Case of the Restless Redhead', Saul's fabricated 'pie sitting' videos) yet receive opposite moral verdicts. He frames this through natural law (Aquinas, Kant) versus legal positivism (Hobbes's command theory, Nietzsche's law as power), the audience's 'God's-eye' perspective, and the means/ends distinction, concluding provocatively that Perry's tampering is actually easier to justify from the positivist side, since he gambles on hunches without knowing his client is innocent, while the show's premises (he is already rich and famous, his clients always innocent) make the material conditions of Saul's lawyering moot for him.

McCrossin reads 'The Case of the Renegade Refugee' (aired December 9, 1961, days before Eichmann's verdict) alongside the film Operation Eichmann and Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem as three competing pop-culture portrayals of the Nazi criminal: monstrous, repentant, and banal. The episode's 'other' refugee, Arthur Hennings/Max Kleinerman, whose Father Paul-inspired 'religious peace' lets him recant on the stand and save Mason's client Harlan Merrill (himself a Battle of the Bulge 'deserter' living a lie created by concussion), supplies what Arendt found absent in Eichmann: empathy and genuine acceptance of guilt, complicating her banality-of-evil picture. The whole is set against the Holocaust as the century's starkest form of the problem of why the innocent suffer while the wicked thrive, and closed with Hogan's Heroes' provocative reuse of the same actors four years later.

Arp uses his own false memory of who pulled the plug at his teenage band's show, the Innocence Project's exoneration statistics (69% involving eyewitness misidentification), and Mason's signature discrediting of confident witnesses (the police chief's tire-track testimony in The Case of the Dubious Bridegroom) to argue eyewitness identification is the deadliest evidence in court. He reviews Loftus's finding that memory is a reconstruction with added information, the Dutch El Al crash study of imagined TV footage, Neisser's Challenger flashbulb-memory study, the Yerkes-Dodson law, and Morgan's high-stress military interrogation study, ending on the paradox that all other courtroom evidence ultimately depends on someone's equally fallible eyes.

book: 134 - KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell
essays: 2. KISStory and Kulture of the Hottest Band in the World
9. KISS the Ship of Theseus Goodbye!
10. KISS Was Made for Lovin’ You
12. An Intimate Look at Paul Stanley’s Love
13. You Wanted the Best, You’ve Got the Right to the Best
14. The Joyful Relativity of Kondoms and Kaskets
15. The Rashomon Effect in KISS’s Autobiographies
16. KISS Goes Disco and Boogies on Simmons’s Bad Faith
18. What Does It Mean if the Band Plays Forever
samples: Editor Courtland Lewis's introduction argues that KISS — the make-up, pyrotechnics, anthems, libido-centered songs, and even the 'Knights in Satan's Service' rumor — makes the band irresistible material for philosophy, quoting Gene Simmons's claim that KISS's original philosophy was 'to create magic and to encourage the suspension of disbelief.' It lays out the volume's structure (sections for the Demon, Space Ace, Starchild, Catman, and Fox) and previews each contributor's chapter, from Siler on the Message to Rentmeester on Kondoms and Kaskets. Lewis closes with personal testimony that KISS's message of perseverance kept him from ever giving up.

R. Alan Siler argues that KISS's deepest and most consistent philosophy is a message of self-belief: work hard, believe in yourself, never give up. He traces it from 'Shout It Out Loud''s 'treat yourself like Number 1' and 'Flaming Youth' through The Elder's oath narrative ('only you are the answer') and its closing declaration 'I believe in me,' to Eric Carr's 'Little Caesar' and Carr's final backing vocals on 'God Gave Rock'n'Roll to You II,' reading Carr's scrappy rise and death as the Message incarnate. Siler contends the Eighties albums are the Message's peak and closes by showing how adherence to it organized his own life accomplishments.

Historian and lifelong fan Matt Alschbach argues that the history of KISS is the history of its fans: his police-officer father taking him to the 1979 San Diego show, schoolyard debates over Alive! versus Alive II, rubbing pencil shadings over the Double Platinum gatefold to guess the band's faces, and strangers' comments on his KISS T-shirts all show the band forging identity and community. He recounts how Alive! rescued Casablanca Records, how the 1983 MTV unmasking and 1996 remasking reinvented the brand for new generations, and how the KISS KRUISE, $50,000 Vault Experience, and Rock & Brews extend its cultural reach. The chapter's claim is that KISS fandom supplies camaraderie, family bonds, and life-meaning across generations.

Courtland Lewis reads Paul Stanley's autobiographies (Face the Music, Backstage Pass) and songs as a worked-out life philosophy. Stanley's turn from chasing approval to confronting his inner pain exemplifies Socrates' unexamined-life dictum; 'Reason to Live' is glossed through Camus's Sisyphus — ground your reason to live in something indestructible, your own self-chosen meaning — while Plato's Ion explains Stanley's mix of learned craft and divine-inspired performance. Aristotle's flourishing through moderation appears in the advice not to overplay 'Rock and Roll All Nite,' and Lewis adds Locke and Rousseau on how laws, boundaries, and education create rather than restrict freedom, closing with Stanley's 'questioning ourselves is not a weakness' as Socratic wisdom.

Donald Presley debunks the claim that KISS are 'Knights in Satan's Service' by showing the pitchfork Satan is a pop-culture invention — tracing the Adversary from the Book of Job through Zoroastrian influence, Dante, and Milton — and arguing that branding Gene's Demon persona or songs like 'God of Thunder' and 'Unholy' as evil commits the informal fallacy of missing the point. He then argues, ironically, that KISS's actual values — hard work, self-empowerment, sexual freedom, indulgence without harming others — overlap substantially with the real LaVeyan Satanism of The Satanic Bible and with Aristotle's ideal of moderately indulging natural goods (sex, alcohol, success) for the sake of flourishing. The conclusion: KISS is not Satanic, but its life-affirming message coincidentally mirrors Satanism's actual teachings, and Christians, KISS, and Satanic virtues can coexist.

Courtland Lewis uses KISS's career gambles to compare theories of decision-making. After Tolstoy's twig-over-the-dragon allegory of mortal life, he tests W.K. Clifford's shipowner (never act without sufficient evidence) against KISS's counter-evidence bet on the Alive! live album, models the choice with Pascal's Wager, and uses the Prisoner's Dilemma to explain the flop of the four 1978 solo albums. He then argues William James's pragmatism — beliefs as rules for action, the living, forced, and momentous option that 'KISS is the best' — best explains why acting on the band's self-created narrative was authentic, with Nietzsche completing the picture: greatness requires leaping, living dangerously, tightrope-walking toward self-defined success.

book: 136 - 30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There
essays: Olympic Tetherball A Final Lesson on Moral Frailty
When Life Gives You Liz’s Lemons, Can You Make Lemonade
Being Gay for Jamie (or, How to Rethink Sexuality)
Liz Meets the Elephant in the Room
Where’s Kenneth We Need to Blame Someone!
“I Truly Don’t Like You as a Person. Can’t One Human Being Not Like Another
The Danger of Thinking “Science Is Whatever We Want It to Be”; or, the
Liz Lemon and High School The More Things Change, the More They Don’t
You Can Take the Man out of Cleveland . .
“Nothing Unusual. Russian Mobs, Invisible Motorcycles, Sex Pooping.”
samples: Editor J. Jeremy Wisnewski argues that Plato, who used the popular dialogue form to draw people into philosophy and filled his dialogues with jokes about self-importance and incompetence, would have been a television writer today. He claims 30 Rock is a modern analogue: a show that imitates a show, just as Plato's Republic is a written speech reporting a fictional dialogue, an imitation twice removed from living philosophical exchange. Invoking Aristotle's claim that philosophy begins in wonder, the introduction frames the book as answers to the questions the TGS writers' room keeps raising about race, the good life, friendship, and knowledge.

The chapter asks whether Kenneth the page is a Kantian rule absolutist who never makes exceptions, or an Aristotelian 'contextual absolutist' who sees that the right act depends on circumstances, as when he runs the Hill Witch ruse to scare Tracy into eating well. Jack's lifeboat hypothetical and rigged-elevator test bounce off Kenneth's refusal to believe in hypothetical situations, but Jack's gift of illegal cable exposes Kenneth's moral frailty when he enjoys the stolen channels. It concludes that Kenneth's gullibility, trust, and loyalty make his simple moral vision both admirable and easily corrupted, and that the real lesson is facing our failures with resolve rather than shame.

Hinzmann reads Liz Lemon's workaholism through Marx and his successors: she gives NBC-Universal-Shinehardt her best years, but her alienation is social and existential rather than the classic alienated labor of the factory, since her creative job leaves her unable to connect with people or to choose love, as with Dennis and Floyd. Drawing on Adorno and the Frankfurt School, the chapter argues Liz cannot see her job as the problem because capitalist ideologies like meritocracy and free will make self-blame feel natural, and the 'Jackie Jormp-Jomp' fight-club episode shows even a life of leisure turns miserable without purpose. Freud's dictum that happiness requires work and love frames the diagnosis: Liz's work gives her life meaning precisely by shutting out everything else that could.

Yim applies Aristotle's three kinds of friendship from the Nicomachean Ethics to the show: Tracy with Grizz and Dot Com in 'Hardball', and Tracy with Jenna in 'Flu Shot', are friendships of utility that dissolve when the benefit ends, while Liz and Jenna's long shared history looks deep but remains mutual usefulness between ambitious colleagues. Liz and Jack, by contrast, evolve from David-versus-Goliath adversaries in the pilot into something like virtuous friendship, culminating in 'Retreat to Move Forward' when Liz humbles herself with a terrible improv routine and a shirt-ripping dance to save Jack's standing before the Six Sigma crowd. The chapter argues the show thereby dramatizes that self-sacrificial goodwill is what makes a friendship worth the risk.

Barkman uses Confucius (ren, yi, li, and zheng ming, treating each person according to what he or she is) and Aristotle (eudaimonia, virtue as a habituated mean between extremes, practical wisdom) to indict 30 Rock for valorizing Jack's 'semi-virtuous path', the smug middle between best and worst announced in 'Do-Over'. He catalogues injustices the show laughs off: Liz's serial lies about her age, hobbies, and adoption; Jack's priority flu shots for the powerful in 'Flu Shot'; Tracy's insubordination about dogfighting in 'Rosemary's Baby'; and Kenneth's servility as everyone's punching bag. On liberality and piety, Jack's confession that 'capitalism is my religion' and Liz's 'I pretty well do whatever Oprah tells me' show the show settling for semi-virtue, which the chapter says even comedy must not endorse.

Wisnewski argues races are socially real but biologically spurious, deploying Appiah's critique of racialism through Tracy's crisis over Dr. Spaceman's DNA results and his dream in which Dream Jefferson tells him 'It's not about who you were. It's about who you are right now.' Fanon's account of the sexual myth of black virility explains why Tracy performs the sex-addicted wildman stereotype while Harvard grad Toofer gets branded not 'really' black. Liz's accidental racism ('Bling bling, that is ghetto fabulous' to Angie, assuming Tracy cannot read) shows racist assumptions operating beneath conscious intent, and the 'Natural Order' equality experiment with Liz and Tracy shows that equal treatment cannot mean identical treatment: equality demands equal consideration of different interests.

book: 137 - Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser
essays: “Some People Have No More Sense Than a Baby!”
A Closer Look at Alice’s Trial
“Language Is Worth a Thousand Pounds a Word”

From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory
samples: Frames the volume with Morpheus's red-pill speech in The Matrix, treating the rabbit-hole as our culture's portal of escape and asking how to make sense of what we find in Wonderland: hookah-smoking caterpillars, babies that turn into pigs, grins without cats, and trials where the sentence comes before the evidence. It takes Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the book's guiding question, tying knowledge of who we are and can become to memory of who we have been, and previews chapters on the feminist Alice, the Red Queen and nuclear strategy, mushroom trips, and the connection between Alice, procrastination, and the Spice Girls.

Argues that Alice, in Carroll's and Disney's versions, is a feminist model who navigates Wonderland by her own wits, unlike passive princesses such as Cinderella and Aurora who need male rescue. Megan S. Lloyd reads Alice's fall down the rabbit-hole as a rejection of her sister's idle female role, the Pigeon's complaints and the Duchess's shaken pig-baby as showing that motherhood is not a requirement of female worth, and the Mad Hatter's 'Then you shouldn't talk' as the old-boy network punishing an assertive woman. Alice's final 'You're nothing but a pack of cards!' completes her growth into a powerful presence, and the chapter closes by asking what twenty-first-century young women facing double standards would do if they asked 'What would Alice do?'

Uses the White Queen's 'jam to-morrow and jam yesterday—but never jam to-day' to introduce Elijah Millgram's jam-yesterday-jam-tomorrow goods: jobs, parenting, and Utah hiking that feel drudging in every moment yet are remembered and anticipated as wonderful. Mark D. White brings in G. E. Moore's organic unity, illustrated by the Spice Girls' 'Wannabe', Wham!, and Led Zeppelin, to ask how a whole made entirely of bad parts can be good 'on the whole', then treats procrastination as akrasia (weakness of will) and endorses Millgram's remedy: manufacture short-term 'jam today' goals like graduation ceremonies and marked lookout points to motivate timely action.

Chases Cold War nuclear strategists down the rabbit-hole, reading the Mad Tea Party as the MAD (mutually assured destruction) tea party where 'to reduce the risk of nuclear war, the risk must be increased' passes for wisdom. Ron Hirschbein uses Wittgenstein's language games (Alice was his favorite English prose), Rorty's final vocabulary, and Derrida's remark that a nuclear war has never 'taken place' to argue that Nukespeak, deterrence, the 'Delicate Balance of Terror', and the post hoc ergo propter hoc argument for deterrence are ungrounded, unfalsifiable word games. The Queen of Hearts's 'Off with his head!' prefigures decapitation strategy and the Hitler card, and the looking-glass chessboard becomes the arms race in which the public are expendable pawns.

Argues Alice is right to attack the court of the King and Queen of Hearts because she never entered a social contract with Wonderland: unlike Socrates, who stayed in Athens and so had to abide by the verdict (Plato's Crito), Alice fell in involuntarily and is trying to leave. Dennis Knepp casts the Queen of Hearts as Hobbes's absolute sovereign whose public 'Off with their heads!' terrorizes the playing cards into obedience ('Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words'), while Locke's limited, consent-based government and Rawls's contractualism mark the better alternative the Hearts court fails to meet. Since Alice stands outside their covenant, she is her own more-than-a-mile-high Leviathan, rightly defending herself in the state of nature.

Splits Wonderland's nonsense into the tolerable kind (strange but lawful regularities, like mushroom side-effects and walking the opposite way to reach the Red Queen, which Alice masters by experiment) and the intolerable kind (the creatures' eristic logic). Using Hume's fork of relations of ideas versus matters of fact, George Dunn and Brian McDonald argue Alice rightly concludes the pig-baby is merely an out-of-the-way matter of fact, while the White Queen's 'jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day' and the King's beheading of the bodiless Cheshire Cat repeat the Sophists' tricks from Plato's Euthydemus, which Socrates deflates from the standpoint of common sense and the examined life. The Knave's trial ('sentence first, verdict afterwards') lands on cable-news pundits who, like the show trials of Stalin, argue from predetermined conclusions.

book: 138 - Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am
essays: “There is nothing in the desert, and no man needs nothing”
This is Rumor Control. Here are the Facts!
Easing Back on the APC’s Throttle
I’m an Alien. And That’s OK
A Professional, a Mother, and Someone Who Cares
Its Structural Perfection is Only Matched by its Autonomy
samples: Book introduction: recounts how the 1979 cast were the first casualties of the Chestburster scene (real butcher-shop organs, Veronica Cartwright fainting), then previews the volume's payload - personhood questions about Ash, Bishop, David and the Ripley clone; Marx on why Weyland-Yutani sacrifices crews for profit; Plato's Republic on children in warfare via Newt; Lovecraftian cosmic horror; feminist readings of Ripley as care ethicist and mother; and continental takes - Xenomorphs as Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Camus on Ripley-8's refusal to commit suicide, and Sartre on a Xenomorph's right to resist us.

Argues David in Prometheus qualifies as a Lockean person - intelligence, rule-following rationality, self-reflection via an active power of thought (his self-modeling on Lawrence of Arabia, his judged desire to be free of Weyland's programming), and mental pleasure and pain - while Ash fails the test, reacting only passively to company orders like Locke's unfree tennis ball. Against Weyland's and Shaw's Cartesian soul-based denial ('you're a robot'), this leaves open that beings humans create could share our moral status, making David's ostracism arbitrary and cruel.

Tests three grounds of moral status against the franchise: species membership (Singer's charge of speciesism - would the human-DNA Newborn count?), Kantian autonomy (which makes Bishop matter but excludes babies and animals, and is itself doubtful once his behavioral inhibitors fix his choices), and Bentham's sentience ('can they suffer?' - Bishop's 'I hurt. Do me a favor. Disconnect me'). Settling on interests and preferences, the chapter argues synthetics with desires - even Ash's admiration for the 'perfect organism' - can be moral patients, so Weyland-Yutani's treatment of them as tools and slaves is wrong.

Uses the Weyland corporations' treatment of crews - Special Order 937, Vickers's 'that makes you an employee,' Burke's Facehugger scheme, the debriefing that mourns a $42 million ship but never the crew - to pit stockholder theory (Friedman, Berle) against libertarian contract theory (Machan) and stakeholder theory (Freeman). The libertarian middle way fails because in deep space crews have neither Hirschman's exit nor voice, so only stakeholder theory explains why hiding workplace hazards and marking employees expendable wrongs them; the market's invisible hand behaves like Ash's very visible murdering hand.

Reads Weyland-Yutani as 'greed is good' cost-benefit reasoning embodied by Ash, Mother, and Burke (Gordon Gekko's Wall Street speech transplanted into space), and asks who can be held accountable when every employee fills only a narrow role and scapegoats absorb blame. It then weighs Kantian deontology - Bishop's inviolable no-harm rules, the absolute wrongness of killing crew for profit - against utilitarian reasoning: Ripley's quarantine refusal to save the many, Parker's refusal to flame the alien holding Lambert, and the uncomfortable thought that acquiring the Xenomorph might genuinely benefit billions.

Diagnoses the Alien universe through Marx's Grundrisse: workers like Parker and Fifield ('I'm here to make money') live only to have and consume, wage labor is avoided like the plague (Pvt. Frost's 'I hate this job'), money replaces the faith people should place in each other, and employees become disposable commodities (Vickers to Shaw: 'that makes you an employee'). Only the conscience-free android Ash fits the Corporation's ideal 'pure capitalist,' and because the saga's future stays capitalist, it vindicates Fukuyama's end-of-history thesis over Marx's prediction of collapse.

book: 139 - Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake
samples: Editor Kristopher Phillips's introduction explains why the Bluths deserve a philosophy book: Buster embodies the academic fear of the perpetual graduate student whose esoteric scholarship (cartography, seventeenth-century agrarian economics) prepares him for nothing, while Tobias is the over-credentialed scholar with no common sense at all, as the 'analrapist' business cards show. The introduction promises that seventeenth-century philosophy and older ideas illuminate everyday life in the O.C. (don't call it that) and might keep readers from emulating Gob's huge mistakes.

Tests Socrates' claim (via Plato's Apology and the Myth of the Cave) that the self-examined life is the happiest against the Bluths: Michael, the one who escapes the cave in the pilot (learning at the boat party that his father is a criminal and he was never getting partnership), turns out chronically miserable, while self-deceivers Gob, Lindsay, and Tobias are mostly content. The chapter concludes that Bertrand Russell's Conquest of Happiness fits better: reflection makes sinners (George Michael's self-loathing over Maeby), narcissists (Michael's need to be seen as good), and megalomaniacs (Kitty) unhappy, so the unexamined life is not a huge mistake, though moderate examination still pays.

Asks what, if anything, makes George Michael kissing Maeby wrong, and dismantles the Argument from Naturalism by testing three definitions of 'natural' against incest, Gob's Segway, and Buster's devotion to Lucille (and Maeby possibly being 'made in a cup' via IVF), showing the argument equivocates in violation of Hume's is/ought distinction. It then weighs Ayer's emotivism (moral claims as 'Yuck!' expressions) against Leon Kass's wisdom of repugnance, concluding the disgust at cousin-kissing may be an aesthetic rather than a moral judgment.

Runs the Bluths through Freudian psychoanalysis: George Sr. hiding in the attic ('Sad Sack', 'Good Grief!') illustrates the unconscious, preconscious, and repression; Michael acts as ego mediating the family's id demands (the unfrozen stock spree) against George Michael's super-ego; Tobias dressing as a pirate among homosexuals and Michael's 'brother...bother' and 'Egg' slips are parapraxes betraying repressed desire; Buster's Motherboy dates and 'Why I Want to Marry My Mother' enact a failed Oedipus complex; and the brothers' scheme against George Sr. in 'Making a Stand' reenacts the primal horde of Totem and Taboo, origin of the incest taboo that haunts George Michael and Maeby.

Uses Sartre's cafe waiter, directly mirrored when Gob play-acts a waiter in 'S.O.B.s', to define bad faith as denying one's freedom by disappearing into roles: illusionist, Bluth Company president in George Sr.'s suit, 'any man' winning back Marta, Ward Cleaver father to Steve Holt (!). Distinguishing bad faith from impossible self-deception (beings-for-themselves have no pre-given essence), the chapter argues that even sincerity ('be yourself, Gob') is bad faith, and provocatively concludes Gob is happier and kinder to others in bad faith, reversing Socrates' 'know thyself'.

Applies Marx's fourfold alienation (from product, from labor, from species-being, from others) to Bluth capitalism: George Michael dips and sells bananas he cannot keep, Lupe cleans Lucille's home under duress, and classes divide the family from the people it exploits. George Sr.'s Boyfights tapes and Caged Wisdom show the capitalist commodifying his children and himself, Gob's figurehead presidency turns employees into resources, Lindsay is 'having without being', and Engels's property-based account of the nuclear family explains Tobias's repressed sexuality; the cure offered is democratic socialism, since within-system fixes only get more absurd.
